speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne contains this paragraph:
As further steps in helping to improve social welfare, co-ordinated plans for rehabilitation of disabled persons are being worked out with the provinces and a measure to facilitate the establishment nation-wide of a federal-provincial assistance program for totally disabled persons will be submitted for your consideration.
Would the Minister of National Health and Welfare tell us what progress has been made in the discussions with the provinces with regard to the establishment of such a nationwide program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROGRESS OF DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING REHABILITATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman's interest in this problem is well known. He was good enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. In reply I can say that on November 10 on behalf of the government I wrote to all the provincial premiers advising them of the intention of the federal government to introduce in this house during the course of the present session legislation that would provide for a nation-wide scheme of dominion-provincial assistance or allowances to totally disabled persons. I have to date received replies from seven provincial governments which indicate that apparently there is genuine satisfaction over the initiative of the federal government, and also their concurrence to a conference to be held in that connection some time in January.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I shall try to keep within the rules.
I realize, of course, that an amendment to the constitution would be required to bring into effect some of the suggestions that I am about to make. I am also aware that promises or suggestions for reform in the past have not resulted in the desired effect. I do not propose to deal with this at length because time does not allow me to go into all the weaknesses, details and ramifications that are apparent. I shall respectfully suggest some remedies.
Let me at the outset say that I am not in favour of the abolition of the other place. That might conceivably be demanded if the present trend of events were to continue. I am also aware of the difficult role which
[Mr. White (Middlesex East) .1

members of the other place have to play in our constitutional set-up; they are the protectors of the rights of minorities. But we find in the other place a large majority of government supporters who are supposed to protect the rights of minorities, both individuals and groups. Occasionally the opposition there is aided by independent Liberal members and I am certain that is appreciated throughout the country.
At the time of confederation the other place was established for the purpose of maintaining a balance, to act as a regulator so that radical legislation would not be forced upon the people. It was established to protect the people and, as I mentioned before, particularly the rights of minorities. Let me say that I know that there will always be minorities in Canada and, as the ramifications of government extend out and out, and as centralization of government grows and grows, the rights of the individual seem to be forgotten. So, I am one of those who are rather perturbed about the trend of events.
The longer I am a member of parliament, the more convinced I am of the need to retain that other place. The longer I am a member the more I see the rights of individuals shoved aside. Speaking of minorities, I believe that at the close of the 1949 election there were in the maritimes over 200,000 people who were in the minority, and there were 205,000 in the province of Quebec. Now, Canadians require a strong upper chamber to review legislation with an unbiased mind and to protect them, as I said, from an all-powerful government. Just on the 19th of this month the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) refused to define "casual labour" as it applied to his department. In other words, in that department one man can be treated differently from another. It just gives you an indication of what is happening in that department and what could happen in many other departments.
In connection with the protection of minorities and individuals, I might just mention that there is a small manufacturer in my riding. During the last year 17 different inspectors from one department of government or another visited his place of business. Each was trying to justify his existence. Those inspectors cannot add anything to the value of a manufacturer's product, but at the same time they can break him.
I am most decidedly against an elected other place. We may enact a very good measure in this house, but it is in the regulations and in the interpretation of the act that loopholes can be found. As is said many times a year, those may be loopholes through which you can drive a horse and carriage.

Dealing with minorities, I think it has already been pointed out that while this government enjoys a very comfortable majority in the house it did not receive 50 per cent of the votes of the people of Canada. Therefore, in a sense, something over 50 per cent of the people are in a minority as far as representation is concerned.
I am going to suggest, sir, that at no time should the opposition in the other house be lower than 25 per cent of the total membership and that at least one-third and preferably one-half of the members should be appointed by the provincial governments in power-the numbers being in direct relation to the population of the area entitled to representation under the constitution. I suggest that all appointments be for a term not to exceed ten years, or until age seventy-five, whichever shall occur first. If this suggestion were followed, the rise and fall of the fortunes of political parties in the provinces and in the dominion would be reflected in the membership of that chamber.
The government now has a mandate from the people for at least four years before there will be another general election. There will be abundant time in which to give this matter some serious thought, and to introduce the amendments required. I therefore ask the Prime Minister and his government to give serious consideration to the plan roughly outlined in order to restore the confidence of the Canadian people in the other place, to ensure to minority groups that their rights will be protected, and to ensure to all individuals the most cherished right under democratic government, namely, the freedom of the individual.
What I had intended also to say in connection with the throne speech has to do with trade, NATO and some of the items mentioned in the throne speech. I want to observe, however, that if it were not for the tragedy of it I would be amused and amazed at the speeches made by some of the government members, both from the maritimes and from the west:	In August they never had it
so good; in November they never had it so bad. Time and again during the twenty-first parliament the opposition warned the government of the dangers of inflation and of the loss of markets for primary products. Now the very things that were warned against are happening.
When the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) mentioned that fish from his province was selling for one cent a pound, the thought just crossed my mind, "I wonder what the consumer is paying for that fish?" and also, "If the spread is great, what are
The Address-Mr. H. O. White the combines investigation people doing about it, if anything?" Recently I was speaking to the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Anderson) and he tells me that fresh fish from his constituency is selling for five cents a pound. When the consumer hears this I imagine he will wonder what is happening from the time the fish is caught until it is in the frying-pan, and I also imagine that what he thinks about it will not be too complimentary.
While I am dealing with the throne speech I want to refer just for a moment to one paragraph. I shall go back to paragraph 6, which reads as follows:
Canada has continued to contribute to those international projects which will promote human welfare and thereby remove some of the causes of unrest and dislocation. You will be asked to approve further assistance for relief and rehabilitation, for technical assistance and for continued participation in the Colombo plan.
I think all hon. members are agreed that we in a favoured nation like this should make as great a contribution as possible to the less fortunate nations, not only for their good but for the cause of democracy and the preservation of our western way of life. On the other hand, I am a bit worried about how we deal with people who are unfortunate here at home. I sometimes think that the old saying, "Charity begins at home", should be taken to heart.
I want to say a word or two about the tornado that visited western Ontario last May and to say to the government that all the people in that area who were affected and who suffered loss are grateful for the grant that was announced by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) last week and for aid from many other agencies. I think if I were going to pick out any one group of persons I should mention the Men-nonites from the Waterloo-Kitchener area who came up there day after day, hired their own transportation and brought their own meals, and contributed greatly to the rehabilitation of those who had suffered such great loss during that tornado.
I took the trouble to inquire into some of the other disasters. I think the Prime Minister will recall my asking some questions back in March of 1951 when there was a vote of $330,000 in the supplementary estimates for the re-construction and the re-equipping of a school at Rimouski following the disastrous fire there. I looked up just what grants had been made to the various areas where disaster of one kind or another had occurred. I find- and I may say that this is all taken from Hansard-that on June 25, 1948, at page 5831 dealing with the Fraser valley, there was a grant of a $5 million lump sum and 75 per
276	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. H. O. White cent of the cost of repairing, strengthening and reconstructing dikes and removing water and debris from flooded lands. On June 23, 1950, there was a vote of $12,500,000 for rehabilitation necessitated by the Red river flood. The reference is page 4083 of Hansard. On June 16, at page 3724 of Hansard, 1950, there was a grant of $2,500,000 from the federal government to be matched by the province. In the recent tornado disaster in western Ontario the federal government held back and left the first step up to the province. But that was not what happened in the instance to which I have referred, as I understand it. The federal government made the grant on the condition that the provincial government would match it, which they did; and I am not finding any fault with that grant. Those people suffered tremendous loss, and as I said in the first place, I think that charity should begin at home. Then on the same date, namely June 16, 1950, there was a grant of $300,000 for Cabano, the amount to be matched by the province, something which also was done. Then on March 18, 1953, with regard to the disastrous floods in Europe, not six months later but almost the next day $1 million was granted for European flood relief. I have no quarrel whatever with that grant.
Upon inquiry last night I found that with all the grants received-county, province, the Canadian disaster relief fund and the grants from the federal government-and they are extremely welcome, the people who suffered loss are still going to be obliged to absorb over 50 per cent of the loss. I took the trouble to inquire from the All Canada Insurance Federation of Montreal just what the losses were in Cabano and Rimouski. I find that of the total losses of almost $7 million, $6 million was paid back from one source or another.
My final comment on that matter is that as far as western Ontario is concerned it was too little and much too late. However, I believe in giving credit where credit is due, and I must give credit to the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin), who has fought the battle for those victims in western Ontario. If it had not been1 for his representations I think that probably the $137,000 which we gratefully received might not have been forthcoming. Before any further disasters happen I think the government should lay down a pattern in consultation with the provinces so that there will be a known formula for the extension of relief immediately. Many of these farmers were not certain whether they were going to get a dollar or 1 per cent, 10 per cent or 75 per cent of their 

losses. Consequently they went through a period of six months not knowing what they could or should do. As I said before, it is too little and too late, and we should lay down a definite formula so that we will know what is going to happen.
I want to deal for a moment with paragraph 7 of the speech from the throne which has to do with defence of the north Atlantic. I am one of those who have said in the past and who still believe that to make such a defence alliance effective and lasting we must also trade with the nations with which we are allied. Trade is the keystone that will bind the bargain as far as our NATO commitments are concerned. While mutual defence pacts are laudable and while we believe in them, an improved and better understanding will follow if we also increase our trade with these nations.
I should like to deal with paragraph 8 of the speech from the throne which reads as follows:
Canada's total volume of external trade has reached record levels but dollar shortages in many countries have persisted and continue to create problems for some of our exporters. Another commonwealth conference with respect to financial and economic matters is to be held in Australia early in the new year.
In recent days newspaper articles have indicated that the United States is prepared to accept sterling in payment for some of its primary products. During the twentieth parliament I advocated that Canada should do that very thing. In the twenty-first parliament, I think in fact during the last session, I again put that idea forward. I pointed out that the government should accept sterling, invest that money in sterling countries and pay our primary producers in dollars. At some time these sterling investments abroad would become convertible and no loss would ensue. In the meantime we would retain for Canadian primary producers a traditional market that we have held for many years.
The action of the United States in being prepared to accept a certain amount of sterling in payment for primary products produced in the United States means, so far as Canada is concerned, but another step in the parade of lost markets. This is going to have an injurious effect. As I mentioned, paragraph 8 of the speech from the throne deals with trade, but the loss of our markets is being reflected in unemployment figures in this country. In addition, some things are taking place with respect to the number of persons unemployed that are not obvious from the unemployment figures. I refer to the fact that many plants are operating short time, some only half time and some less than that. Some plants that employed two or three hundred

men are now operating with less than a hundred. Thus loss of trade is reflected in loss of jobs.
I have mentioned before in the house that inflation has played a large part in the loss of markets because with the coming of inflation and increasing prices we have priced ourselves out of many European markets. Another factor that is very disturbing is the fact that unfair trade practices on the part of the United States have resulted in the banning of many Canadian products from that country. As Canadians we all welcomed the visit to Canada and to this chamber of President Eisenhower, and I think we were all impressed with the sincerity with which he emphasized how important it was that relations between our two countries should continue to be friendly and that this friendship should increase as time goes on.
But I respectfully suggest that such actions on the part of the United States are contrary to the Geneva trade agreements to which the United States was a signatory. They have not lived up to the agreements. We also find our textile industry being forced to lay off help and losing markets because of the dumping not of textiles from other foreign countries but of textiles from our next door neighbour, the United States, which dumping is robbing Canadian workmen of jobs and pay. What about suggesting to the United States that they honour their signature to the Geneva and subsequent agreements? What about dumping textiles on the Canadian market and thus threatening the livelihood of thousands of Canadian workmen and their families? Is the policy of the government again to be too little and too late?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I wish first of all to extend to you, sir, my sincere congratulations on your unanimous election to your high office. May I be permitted to say that you have given convincing proof of your ability to preside over our deliberations with dignity, urbanity, considerateness and impartiality. We are indeed fortunate in our choice. I trust that all our decisions will be equally wise and happy.
I should also like to associate myself with the well-deserved tributes which have been paid to the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply, the hon. member for York Centre and the hon. member for Roberval. I feel confident that I am expressing the sentiments of all present when I venture to predict that the future of parliamentary democracy is assured in Canada as long as young men of the high
The Address-Mr. A. M. Fraser calibre of these two hon. members continue to offer themselves for election to our House of Commons.
I also wish, Mr. Speaker, to take advantage of this occasion to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the decisive victory of the government in the general election last August. In my opinion the result of that election was a signal vote of confidence on the part of the Canadian people in the sound and farsighted policies which the Liberal administration has been pursuing both at home and abroad under his wise and vigorous leadership. Like other hon. members who have spoken from this side of the house, I am very conscious of the fact that I owe my election, in no small measure, to the prestige of his name. I wish to thank him for the invaluable support accorded me by his visit to St. John's where he spoke on my behalf. The Prime Minister is one of the truly great world statesmen of our time, and I am indeed proud to serve under such a leader.
I am proud too to represent the federal riding of St. John's East, and I wish to thank the voters of that historic district for having elected me to this house. St. John's East, Mr. Speaker, is a compact and well-balanced constituency. It has diversified economic interests. Among these are commerce, shipping, manufacturing, mining, agriculture, and fishing. Approximately half of the population of the riding live in St. John's proper. The other half live on Bell island in rural settlements along the beautiful shores of Conception bay and along the rugged but picturesque Atlantic coast line north of St. John's. My constituents include sturdy fishermen of such typical fishing settlements as Logy Bay, Bauline and Pouch Cove. They include the hard-working farmers in that area from Paradise to Marysvale, all of whom, I regret to say, are at present passing through a very difficult period because of the competition of low-priced food crops from the mainland provinces. They include also the skilled workers in several new manufacturing plants which form part of what I may call the diamond horseshoe of industry, which extends along the coast from Conception bay, not only in the riding which I have the honour to represent, but in that represented by my friend the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick). These new industrial plants, and many others in other parts of Newfoundland, have been established through the initiative of the provincial government under the leadership of Premier Smallwood, with the object of broadening the base of the island's economy.

The Address-Mr. A. M. Fraser
Alongside these new industries stand the long-established mining operations on Bell island with their virtually unlimited deposits of iron ore. I was very sorry to learn, from the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), that there is widespread unemployment among the coal miners of Glace Bay. We in St. John's East feel we are bound by close ties of sympathy to the hon. member's riding, for as the hon. member knows the Bell island iron mines are operated by Dominion Wabana Ore Limited, a subsidiary of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company, and the iron ore of Bell island helps to feed Dosco's steel mills at Sydney, Nova Scotia.
Bell island too has had its ups and downs, but I am glad to be able to inform the house that the production of iron ore at Bell island is now being well maintained and that the industry is affording full employment at good wages. Far from pursuing a restrictive policy on Bell island, the company has recently embarked on an impressive program of mechanization and modernization of its equipment. I hold no brief for the company, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, in the past, it has not displayed any conspicuous sense of public responsibility; but it is only fair to add that it is now showing a greater interest than hitherto in the welfare of the Bell island community. It has begun negotiations with the federal government for the construction of an airstrip on Bell island, and I understand that the maritime headquarters of the air transport board has undertaken to make a survey of the proposed site within the next month in order to decide upon its feasibility.
The construction of an airstrip on Bell island has, in my opinion, much to recommend it. It would reduce the isolation from which Bell island suffers in the winter and early spring when communication with Portugal Cove is rendered hazardous by ice and heavy seas. It would also provide a landing ground which could be used as an alternate to the T.C.A. terminal at Torbay airport in case of emergency. The company, I understand, is also consulting with the provincial government of Newfoundland in an effort to improve housing conditions on Bell island.
The urban section of the riding comprises the eastern part of the city of St. John's. It is there that the foundations of the British Empire were laid, for it was there in 1583, on King's beach, that that dauntless but ill-fated adventurer and explorer, Sir Humphrey Gilbert, took possession of the New Found Land in the name of his sovereign, Queen Elizabeth I. By royal proclamation Newfoundland was formally declared to belong to
tMr. Fr;>r". 'St. John's East).]

England and1 was recognized as the first colonial possession of the crown. That is why Newfoundland came to be known as Britain's oldest colony. Thus, 370 years ago, the cornerstone of the commonwealth was laid in what is now the capital city of Canada's tenth province. St. John's therefore provides a link between the spacious days of the first Elizabeth and the reign of our beloved Queen Elizabeth II.
For the citizens of St. John's, therefore, the coronation of Her Majesty, to which such felicitous reference has been made in the speech from the throne, has had a special significance, and they share with Her Majesty's loyal subjects everywhere the hope that the new reign will usher in another golden age for all her people.
It is a source of great satisfaction to free men everywhere that the forces of the United Nations have repelled the aggressors in Korea, and that the carnage there has been halted by a truce. I am sure that all hon. members will endorse the hope, firmly expressed in the speech from the throne, that a political conference will ultimately succeed in restoring peace to Korea. At present however it is well for us to remember that all that has been achieved there as yet is a truce, and a somewhat uneasy truce at that, but a truce of which I feel it may be said, as was said of the peace of Amiens, that it is a truce of which everybody was glad but of which nobody was particularly proud.
It is indeed very true, as was stated in the speech from the throne, that much remains to be done before there can be a permanent and durable peace in the world. That being so, the speech from the throne rightly emphasizes the need for the free nations to continue their efforts to build' up and maintain the necessary strength to deter aggression. In this vital task Canada has, I believe, a major role to play, and one which I feel confident she will play all the more effectively because of the strategic importance of her new province. During the second world war Newfoundland was transformed into the Gibraltar of the west, bristling with naval and air bases which were to play a decisive part in winning the all-important battle of the Atlantic. St. John's harbour, although too small to be used as an assembly point for convoys, proved an excellent convoy escort base for destroyers and frigates. St. John's also rendered very valuable service as a haven of refuge for ships striken by enemy submarines, and as a port of succour for survivors suffering from wounds and exposure.
Aircraft of the Royal Canadian Air Force, based on the great airports of Torbay and Gander, provided an umbrella of air power

for convoys over a vast expanse of the ocean to points where air coverage could be continued by planes operating from Iceland and the Azores. Thus, Newfoundland became, as it were, an unsinkable aircraft carrier guarding the western convoy routes against the ravenous packs of U-boats. She also became one of the sally-ports of freedom for many of the bombers which dominated the skies over Germany, and which, like an avenging host from out of the West, were ferried across the broad Atlantic to Britain, either direct from Gander or by way of Greenland and Iceland from Goose Bay in Labrador.
This brief historical sketch may serve to remind the house of Newfoundland's great strategic value in the recent past. Her strategic importance has not been diminished by post-war developments in sea and air power. The increased cruising range of the super-submarines of today has intensified the threat to the Atlantic lifeline between North America and western Europe. Therefore, in the tragic event of a third world war-which God forbid-the need for an advanced base for the escort of convoys, a base situated one-third of the way across the Atlantic from the North American continent, would be even more imperative than it was a decade ago. Atomic attacks on North America by jet-propelled aircraft would be a virtual certainty. Fighter aircraft, based in Newfoundland, could intercept hostile bombers en route across the Atlantic and harry them while still at a considerable distance from the North American mainland. Similarly, fighter aircraft, stationed at Goose airport in Labrador, could help in repulsing or at least disorganizing trans-polar air attacks along the Arctic approaches to Canada.
Newfoundland's strategic position made a most valuable contribution to the winning of the second world war. It may well be that she is destined to make an equally valuable contribution to the establishment and preservation of a real and lasting peace. The speech from the throne states that:
The alliance of the North Atlantic nations has been effective thus far in preventing aggression in Europe.
Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, is a strong link in the chain of defence with which the signatories of that treaty are girdling the North Atlantic region.
I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to the question which is of paramount importance to the whole of Newfoundland, namely, the future of her fishing industry. First of all, I would like to assure the government that its scheme whereby the fishermen can insure their boats and gear has met with wholehearted approval in Newfoundland. It is a great boon to our
The Address-Mr. A. M. Fraser fishing industries. It is helping to combat the insecurity arising from the hazards of wind and wave.
There is, however, another source of insecurity against which our fishermen need protection even more, the economic insecurity which is caused by lost markets and low prices.
In the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker, the house has heard a great deal about the problems which farmers of the prairie provinces are encountering in marketing their wheat. I hasten to inform the house that we in Newfoundland have our marketing problems also. Dollar shortages in our Mediterranean markets and in Brazil have severely curtailed the effective demand for our salt codfish and have seriously depressed the price level. Indeed, the situation has become so acute that, only last month, our provincial government was obliged to make an advance of $1.50 a quintal to our fishermen in an effort to bridge the gap between this year's prices and the higher prices obtained last year. This, however, is only a short term expedient. To achieve a real solution of the fisheries problem, long range measures are necessary.
It was, therefore, with keen satisfaction that I read the following passage in the speech from the throne, and I quote:
My government is giving particular attention to the development of markets for our fisheries and to the encouragement of more modern methods in the Atlantic coast fisheries, particularly in the province of Newfoundland where the methods are in the greatest need of improvement.
Hon. members are probably aware, Mr. Speaker, that an important report on the Newfoundland fisheries was published a few months ago. It was a report prepared by a committee of experts appointed under the auspices of the federal government and the government of Newfoundland. This committee, presided over by Sir Albert Walsh, the Chief Justice of Newfoundland, made far-reaching recommendations for the more scientific utilization of our fishery resources, and for the transformation of the social and economic life of our fishermen. The implementation of these recommendations would mean a new deal for the fishermen of Newfoundland. Failure to implement them might well spell the doom of Newfoundland's fishing industry. Already the industry is being deserted by the youth of our island. It cannot long support this drain on its lifeblood.
The earnings and working conditions of our fishermen must be made more attractive if the industry is to survive and prosper. The Walsh report points the path to recovery. But the expenditure involved will cost many

This social and humanitarian legislation could have found no better sponsor than the Prime Minister. Surrounded by men of undisputed ability he will continue to give this country that magnificent forward impulse which will ensure its continued progress. He has shown himself to be a great exponent of peace and democracy and for this reason he enjoys not only on this continent, but everywhere in Europe, after only a few short years of public life, a reputation equalled by only a few statesmen.
Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Rimouski has no fault to find with the administration of this country in the past years. May I nevertheless be allowed to say that in social security payments alone the Department of National Health and Welfare, in the past four years, has distributed, in my constituency, more than $10,000,000. Mr. Speaker, I should like also to congratulate the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. NOVEMBER 24, 1953
Pearson) for having appointed Mr. Jules Leger as ambassador to Mexico. I would like to be allowed a few more minutes, Mr. Speaker, in order to say a word or two about my county. Everybody seems to know Rimouski, and more particularly so since the catastrophic conflagration which destroyed half the city. Since May 6, 1951, that part which had been laid waste has been rebuilt, thanks to gifts from various governments, and from numerous charitable souls, thanks also to the remarkable courage displayed by the victims. I seize this opportunity to thank the federal government for the two and a half million dollars they gave to those who suffered from the disaster, so that they might build themselves new homes. But one should not think mistakenly that this gift and the other gifts-no more than the various insurances-have made good the losses. In fact, these losses have exceeded $25,000,000, while the relief assistance was no more than about half that sum. The conflagration may have made Rimouski famous abroad, but we must not forget that this publicity has cost the victims an over-all sum of about $12,000,000.
The county of Rimouski, which lies halfway between Quebec and Gaspe, comprises three cities: Trois Pistoles, Rimouski and Mont Joli and includes, besides, several lovely agricultural parishes. Mont Joli is endowed with a splendid airport which, during the last war, was used for the training of airmen from all over the commonwealth and which, since then, has been used mostly by civil aviation. This airport built by the government in my county is today one of the reasons for the growth of the city of Mont Joli. It seems to me that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not bring this fact to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton).
In case of another war, I could not object if the Canadian air force were to be based
The Address-Mr. Legare there, but I would think it my duty to ask that civil aviation continue to use that airport. So, if the Minister of National Defence were to contemplate the possibility of having to mobilize completely the Mont Joli airport, in case of international complications or even for the peacetime training of airmen, I would ask him to so inform the Department of Transport for, as I say, it is necessary for the economy of Mont Joli that landing strips remain available to civil aviation.
Rimouski also has its own airport, though it is not quite so large, and I want to thank the Minister of Transport who is having a landing strip built there. Rimouski also has an important sea harbour which is largely used by coastal and transatlantic craft. Seafaring activities are progressing every year, and that is why I would need the co-operation of the Department of Public Works for the expansion of navigational facilities. I also am counting on the help of that department in developing the shipyard which is now being built at Rimouski and which is doubtlessly needed in the whole eastern part of Quebec.
I also would like to draw the attention of the Public Works Department to the necessity of developing other harbours or seaports in my county. The harbour of Trois Pistoles in particular would need to be planned in such a way as to be able to receive vessels of higher tonnage; the one at Pointe-au-Pere has urgent need of a shelter where ferries may be accommodated in gales and stormy weather.
Mr. Speaker, the time that is granted me today does not allow me to mention the other parishes in my county and to underline their most pressing needs. I shall certainly have an opportunity to do so some other time. However, I would like to draw the attention of the department right now to the consequences which would follow the realization of a project which has been under study for a few years now and whose object

My last request is for the construction without any delay of a railway on the north shore of the Gaspe peninsula. I do not wish to intrude into the field of action of my friend the member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois) but I feel it would be in the interest of the entire country to give that district the benefit of railway service. However, that beautiful region, which is visited by thousands of tourists each year and which is perhaps the most beautiful part of Canada, has now reached the stage where the construction of a railway is necessary. It is now an economic necessity, and the growth of this district depends a great deal upon it. I therefore suppose that the Minister of Transport will give the matter further consideration without delay and will soon announce its realization.

Mr. Speaker, it appears to be customary, speaking in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to mention a wide range of subjects, and particularly for freshmen members to speak of their own ridings. In a moment or two I shall do this rather briefly. It is not my purpose to take up the time of the house in uttering a lot of platitudes; but there are certain achievements of the people in the county of Perth and some grave conditions now existing which I feel should be brought to the attention of hon. members.
Before making these observations however I should like to join previous speakers in passing on congratulations through you, sir, to Mr. Speaker. As a newcomer to the house, it is amazing to find how all the knowledge, experience and tact necessary for the proper fulfilment of the great responsibilities of that high office could be centred in one member. If it does not appear too brash on my part as a newcomer, I should like to say that I believe Mr. Speaker does possess those qualities.
And I would also congratulate you, sir, upon your elevation to your present position of Deputy Speaker. It was my good fortune to be associated with you during school days. Looking back I seem to recall that even then you displayed those qualities which now enable you to carry out your duties so admirably.
May I say just a word or two about my thoughts upon arriving here in Ottawa as the duly elected member in the House of Commons for the riding of Perth. I do not think any freshman at a university ever felt more like a freshman than I did on that particular morning. However, owing to the friendship, advice and suggestions offered by members on both sides of the house, I now feel somewhat more at home.
When I look at the map of this great Canada of ours and realize that I am one of the 265 persons sent here to govern the country, I feel very humble. I think we should all sit back and look at that map occasionally so that we may not lose that feeling of humility.
I should like to reiterate the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) last Friday when he said:	jj (
This is a moment, Mr. Speaker, which I am not likely soon to forget, in rising for the first time to take part in a debate in the House of Commons.
And now a few words concerning my home city of Stratford and my riding of Perth. We are situated in the middle of the garden of

Canada. I think that, aside from our geographical location, this statement is borne out by the results of the recent elections. We are practically surrounded by ridings which saw fit either to return sitting members or to elect to the house new members who represent the party of which I am a supporter.
My constituency, which since the redistribution of 1933 has been known as Perth, formerly constituted two ridings, namely those of North Perth and South Perth. This county in the past has sent many illustrious members to Ottawa. It is my fervent hope that I shall be as faithful and industrious in fulfilling my duties as were my predecessors. Incidentally, I trust I may be excused for mentioning that my paternal grandfather represented North Perth in the House of Commons from 1873 to 1878. During that period, unfortunately, he also sat to the left of the Speaker. I am confident, sir, that, if I may use a slang expression, I shall enjoy going that gentleman one step better and having the experience of moving to the other side of the chamber.
We have in Stratford many manufacturing concerns. Time will not permit me to speak at length about all these business enterprises, of which we are justly proud. I should like however to say something to the house about our largest employer of labour, the Canadian National Railways. We have an investment by the C.N.R. in Stratford amounting to many millions of dollars, in the way of buildings and equipment provided for the repair of steam locomotives. I am greatly concerned about the future of these repair shops, and I do beseech consideration by the management of the Canadian National Railways by way of planning for the future use of these facilities. Since August 10 of this year there have been at least two and, if I am not mistaken, three separate lay-offs of employees. It has been intimated by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that these lay-offs are temporary; I can only trust that he is right.
This is serious for us. We feel that, because of the gradual dieselization of this system, unless planning for the future is begun now we are only going to suffer more and more lay-offs. As you may know, the Canadian Pacific Railway recently commenced a new fast diesel service between Toronto and Windsor. Will the present service which the Canadian National provides be able to compete successfully with this? I do not think so. This is a huge, continuously growing Canada and I suggest that the management of the Canadian National grow with the 83276-19
The Address-Mr. Monteith country. Let it develop new ideas to attract passenger revenue and improve freight service.
Surely in an expanding economy such as ours the Stratford Canadian National repair shops do not have to face a gradual reduction in employment simply because the system is becoming dieselized. As dieselization of the system progresses I urge the government to give early consideration to the use that will be made of the facilities provided by the Stratford shops, which facilities represent such a huge investment.
A particularly important attainment in the history of Stratford and of Canada materialized this past summer. I am speaking now of the Stratford Shakespearean festival. That festival was the greatest cultural achievement Canada has ever experienced. Unfortunately its production coincided somewhat with another interesting event in Canada this summer, in that it commenced early in July and ran through until after August 10. Most of us were, I think excusably so, very busy and probably could not find time to attend the festival. I believe it was on July 28 when the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did squeeze in sufficient time to visit Stratford and incidentally the festival. I only hope he does not now feel that the time thus consumed was at all ill spent.
This festival originated in the mind of a Stratford young man by the name of Tom Patterson. He dreamed of such an undertaking for some time and finally convinced a number of the citizens of Stratford that he had something. This was a terrific decision to make, and I should like to congratulate particularly the promoter and those citizens who gave so unstintingly of their time and energy in the early stages of the production.
I should like to take a few moments of the time of this house to read a few of the objects of the Stratford Shakespearean festival foundation of Canada which was incorporated under the laws of the province of Ontario on October 31, 1952:
1.	To promote interest in, and the study of, the arts generally and literature, drama and music in particular.
2.	To advance knowledge and appreciation of and to stimulate interest in Shakespearean culture and tradition by theatrical performances and otherwise.
3.	To provide for facilities for education and instruction in the arts of the theatre.
4.	To provide improved opportunities for Canadian artistic talent.
5.	To advance the development of the arts of the theatre in Canada.

The Address-Mr. Monteith
There is no doubt that the future of this festival is now assured. I feel that all culturally-minded people in Canada are grateful to those few in Stratford who had the foresight and initiative to make it possible.
I should like to present just a few statistics to show what effect this festival had upon the economy of Stratford and Canada as a whole. A total of 68,800 tickets were sold, 38 [DOT] 1 per cent being sold in the United States. Canadian National ticket sales from Toronto to Stratford were up 55 per cent during July and August, 1953 over the same period in 1952. Bank clearances were up over $3,850,000 during June, July and August, 1953 as compared with the corresponding period in 1952. It will be remembered that this is a city of approximately 19,000 people. Cars were parked in the festival parking lot from nine provinces in Canada and 35 states of the union to the south.
I trust that my words about this undertaking have not taken up too much of the time of the house. If we are through our business in time next summer I do hope every hon. member will avail himself of the opportunity of visiting Canada's greatest cultural achievement, the Stratford Shakespearean festival.
The other day the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) mentioned in the house that his city possesses the finest water supply in Canada. I would respectfully take issue with that statement as undoubtedly the city of Stratford has that distinction. Our water comes from deep wells and possesses fluorine in exactly the correct quantities as they have been determined up to now. Comparisons have been made with other cities in Canada as to dental conditions, and I think the statistics resulting from those comparisons are favourable to my contention. I shall not burden hon. members with the details. A letter was written by the Department of National Health and Welfare to the medical officer of health of Stratford under date of April 29, 1949. One paragraph of this letter reads:
Stratford is to be congratulated upon its good fortune in having among its children what probably is the best dental condition of any city in Canada. The caries attack rate is more than two-thirds less than in the average Canadian city. It is believed that this is due to the fact that the Stratford water supply, as well as being excellent, contains from its natural sources, 1-3 PPM of flourine.
I feel that letter supports my view that Stratford possesses a quality of water beyond comparison.
I should like to mention that in Stratford as well as in other communities of Perth


county there are several depressed textile industries. These industries, along with dairy machinery manufacturers, appear to be suffering from unfair dumping on our markets from abroad. I expect there will be an opportunity later to discuss these matters.
I have not thus far made any mention of the wonderful farming country surrounding Stratford, nor of the towns and villages of Perth county. The welfare of those towns and villages, as well as the welfare of Stratford, depends to a large extent upon trade with the farming districts. May I point out that Perth county is in the midst of one of the best mixed farming districts in Canada. We have farmers concentrating on dairy cattle and dairy products, on beef cattle, on grains, on cash crops such as sugar beets, on poultry, on fur-bearing animals and on several other specialties. Many of these farmers have legitimate complaints which I feel should command our attention.
The drop in grain prices has been considerable, and this matter has been discussed at some length in this chamber. As a consequence I do not propose to enlarge on the subject. At some future date I may find it necessary to climb aboard with the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) and go for a ride on the sugar beet question.
I should like to bring to your attention the plight of the farmer who has been fattening beef cattle which he bought at say 29 cents a pound, who has been feeding them for several months and then has been forced to sell at say 19 cents per pound in order to meet bank loans. Such an operation cannot have any result other than financial ruin. Then there is the dairy farmer whose monthly milk cheque up until a comparatively short time ago was perhaps $350, but who is now receiving possibly $200. Such a man is in anything but a happy state of mind.
I should like to speak briefly concerning the cheese industry. The hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Follwell) has claimed that the best cheese produced anywhere in Canada comes from his riding, but in my opinion Perth county has attained the position of producing cheese of a quality second to none. Reports concerning sediment in milk going into cheese production do, I am sure, bear out this contention.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I cannot share the hon. member's enthusiasm for the part the present government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have played in the marketing of cheese. True, the Liberal government did buy 5J million pounds of cheese of last year's make; but was it not still

in Canada? Recent sales to Britain have left the whole industry in a much healthier condition. These sales have achieved the result of assuring the removal of 10 million pounds of cheese from the Canadian market. May I point out that these recent sales to Britain were made by the Ontario cheese marketing board without assistance from the federal government or the Minister of Agriculture. The cheese market has now firmed considerably, and the whole dairy industry will benefit from the fact that this deal was made in a straight businesslike manner without government interference.
May I conclude by stressing that many such benefits would accrue under an economy of free competition.
