There is a special class of workers on whose behalf I have always fought and shall keep on fighting.
Labour unions provide, through their joint committees, for agreements between management and labour, for the drafting of contracts that set the salary rate to be paid to the different tradesmen. But there is still one category of workers who have not yet been able to form a strong organization-and I believe they would be well advised to do so- that would strive to obtain for them a reasonable salary, to which they are entitled. I am speaking of that group commonly referred to as the white-collar workers, the clerical employees and more particularly the people employed by governments, whether it be at the municipal, the provincial or the federal level, who are not getting, in my opinion, the salaries they should be getting. I am not blaming the federal government more than any other, but I believe, Mr. Speaker, that a commission should be established to investigate seriously the salary paid to some employees.
I am told that some employees doing the same kind of work as others in other departments are not receiving the same rate of pay. I know that the federal government is more unjust than others in that field. However, we are not aiming at doing worse than others, but better. I think that, if you compare salaries paid by the federal government and those paid by the government of my province, you will realize that the former is more generous. However, I believe that there is still room for improvement. Wage scales of various categories of salaried people should be examined, such as secretaries, statisticians and others, who, in fact, are not treated on the same basis in all departments. I heard somebody mention store clerks. Well, I feel that if I were a store clerk, a white-collar worker in a private industry, I would start a movement in order to set up an organization, because I am sincerely convinced that the situation is alarming. It is lawful for them to organize, except for the civil servants of my province who are not free to assert their rights, or to submit their rightful claims.


I am however speaking generally since I am not among those who have set themselves the task of being the uncompromising opponents of the working people. I speak for industry in general and I do believe that these people would be well advised to form associations since they have a perfect right to do so and this would be to their advantage.
Certain industries pay their employees very well indeed; fortunately so, and I would like to remind the government of some of its own employees in the various departments, who are not all treated in the same way.
There is another question. I would have liked to discuss it at greater length, but, after all, time is limited and I still have two or three little points to submit to the government. I would like to suggest to the government-and there is no time like the present to do so since the Criminal Code is to be revised-that they consent to an amendment to the Criminal Code which would allow for a national lottery. I am in favour of a national lottery for a number of reasons. I cannot understand that such a thing can be allowed -besides, the words I am now uttering are not new, they are very old arguments often resorted to-I cannot understand that one may legally bet on a horse race, while it is not permitted to buy a lottery ticket to allay misery and at the same time help our hospitals. I cannot understand that people earn $50,000 or $140,000-lucky people-and are not-I do not say they should, mind you- be prosecuted. I fail however to understand such an attitude since they commit an act forbidden by the Criminal Code. They nevertheless win fabulous sums of money. Once again, I do not wish to speak for the case of those who would like to see these people prosecuted in accordance with the law. They hit the jackpot, they do not pay any income tax although it is the result of an illegal act. The result of this anomaly is that the European hospitals reap all the millions, which they get each year, while our hospitals have to rely on grants and donations. I have not the figures here, but I do not think I am wrong in saying that, as a result of different subscription campaigns, there were paid in, during the last five or six years, no less than $50 million in the city of Montreal alone, in subscriptions to hospitals. We went and begged that money from the industrialists, from everyone. In speaking for a national lottery I do not ask that we do away with private charity. But if we can give a few more millions to the hospitals, these subscrip-

tion campaigns could be maintained, because we all realize the great need for beds, which is at the present time the major problem of our hospitals. More than ever we need hospitals for tuberculosis, cancer cases or any other diseases. So, if we were to give our hospitals these millions which go out to Europe, it seems to me that we would do something splendid. I hope I shall not shock any of the hon. members in stating that I have seen how people holding high positions in our universities and in our schools carefully hide the lottery ticket they have purchased, while loudly denouncing the scandal of a national lottery which, according to them, would legalize what they brand as gambling. I am
The Address-Mr. Dupuis even told that some members of the House of Commons buy lottery tickets. I do not know if it is true but I maintain that it is possible. I would be loath to blame those who indulge in such activities; but while this lottery has millions of subscribers, I wonder why we could not, once and for all, legalize public subscription to this type of humanitarian project.
